The 15% that never comes back: US dividend withholding tax in an RRSP, a TFSA and a taxable account

US stocks pay dividends after US tax is withheld, and whether you ever get that tax back depends on the account and on how you hold the stocks. Compare a Canadian-listed fund with a US-listed ETF in an RRSP, a TFSA and a taxable account, see how a small yearly drag compounds, and find when currency conversion costs outweigh it.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Where US dividend withholding tax sticks: RRSP, TFSA or taxable account, US-listed ETF or Canadian fund

$100,000 of US stocks yielding 1.5% a year, with prices rising 5% a year and dividends reinvested yearly. US tax is withheld at 15% unless the holder is an RRSP or RRIF that owns US-listed securities directly, which the Canada–US tax treaty exempts. Inside a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, and inside any Canadian-listed fund, the withholding is not recovered. In a taxable account it is credited against Canadian tax on the same dividend, assumed here to be enough to absorb it. Shortfalls are measured against the same stocks with no withholding and no conversion cost, inside the account and before any tax on RRSP withdrawals. A US-listed ETF pays 1% to convert dollars in and again to convert them out. Fund fees, currency movements and tracking differences are left out; returns are hypothetical, not a forecast.

The central idea

US withholding of 15% on dividends is recovered in a taxable account through the foreign tax credit, is avoided by an RRSP or RRIF holding US-listed securities directly, and is lost everywhere else: in a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, and inside any Canadian-listed fund. On a 1.5% yield the loss is about 0.23% a year, a real but modest cost that compounds. Converting currency to avoid it costs money too, so the right choice depends on yield, conversion cost, fees and how long you hold, not on the withholding alone.

01

A small line on the statement

Someone who holds US stocks, through an index fund, an ETF or a balanced fund with a US equity sleeve, receives dividends that have already been cut. The United States taxes dividends paid to foreign investors at source, and for Canadian residents the Canada–US tax convention caps that tax at 15% of the gross dividend for ordinary portfolio holdings (Article X, paragraph 2(b)).

Whether that 15% is a real cost depends on two things this guide separates: the account, whose tax rules decide whether the withholding can be credited, and the structure of the holding, which decides who the US treats as the shareholder. The tool below follows the same US stocks held four ways and measures what the withholding, and the currency conversion some people use to avoid it, costs over time.

The amounts are smaller than most fund fees, and that is the first lesson. Withholding tax is worth understanding and arranging sensibly; it is rarely worth taking on extra risk, concentration or complexity to avoid.

02

The rules in four sentences

  1. Taxable account. US dividends are foreign income, taxed in full at your marginal rate. The US tax withheld is generally credited against the Canadian tax on that income through the federal foreign tax credit, so the withholding is not an extra cost as long as you owe at least that much Canadian tax on it. A Canadian fund passes the foreign income and the foreign tax it paid to you on the T3 slip (boxes 25 and 34), CRA explains, so the credit works through a fund too.
  2. RRSP or RRIF, US-listed securities. Article XXI, paragraph 2 of the treaty exempts dividends and interest received by an arrangement “operated exclusively to administer or provide pension, retirement or employee benefits”. RRSPs and RRIFs are treated as such arrangements, so a US-listed ETF or US share held directly in them normally pays its dividends without withholding.
  3. TFSA, FHSA or RESP. These are not retirement trusts for treaty purposes. CRA warns that foreign dividends paid to a TFSA or an FHSA could be subject to foreign withholding tax, and its foreign tax credit folio (¶1.69) says foreign tax on income earned in an RRSP or TFSA does not count for a foreign tax credit. The 15% is simply lost.
  4. Any Canadian-listed fund holding US stocks. The fund, a Canadian trust, is the shareholder. It suffers the 15% itself, whatever account you hold its units in. In a taxable account it can pass the credit to you; in an RRSP, TFSA or other registered plan nothing can recover it.

A further layer applies when a Canadian-listed fund holds a US-listed ETF that in turn holds stocks outside the US: foreign taxes withheld by those other countries at the bottom level are also lost, and are not shown here.

03

Chart 1: one year of dividends, four ways

With the defaults, $100,000 of US stocks yielding 1.5% pays $1,500 of dividends in the first year. The first chart follows that $1,500.

In an RRSP holding a US-listed ETF, all of it is reinvested. In an RRSP holding a Canadian-listed fund, or in a TFSA, FHSA or RESP holding either kind, $225 is withheld and never returns, and $1,275 is reinvested. In a taxable account the $225 is also withheld, but it counts toward the $444.75 of Canadian tax due on the dividend at a 29.65% marginal rate; you pay the remaining $219.75, and $1,055.25 is left to reinvest.

The taxable account loses the most to tax in that year, but not because of withholding: foreign dividends are fully taxed as income in Canada. The registered accounts shelter the dividend from Canadian tax; only the US share stays behind. Keep the comparison straight: the RRSP figures are before the tax due when money is eventually withdrawn, and a TFSA withdrawal is tax-free.

04

Chart 2: a small yearly drag compounds

The withholding takes yield × rate from the holding every year: 1.5% × 15% = 0.225% a year with the defaults. That looks tiny, but money lost early never grows. Against the same stocks with no withholding, which grow to about $482,770 over 25 years at 5% price growth plus 1.5% dividends, a Canadian-listed fund in an RRSP or TFSA ends about $24,862 lower, around 5% of the ending value.

A US-listed ETF avoids the withholding only in an RRSP or RRIF, and it needs US dollars. At a conversion cost of 1% each way, converting in and converting back takes about 2% of the money, about $9,607 by year 25 on the larger ending balance. In a TFSA the US-listed ETF pays both the conversion and the withholding, and falls furthest behind, about $33,975.

None of these figures includes fees. Many Canadian-listed US index funds and their US-listed equivalents differ in management fee by a few hundredths of a percent a year, which over 25 years can be as large as the effects shown. Compare the whole cost, not one line.

05

Chart 3: when the conversion cost pays for itself

In an RRSP the real trade-off is between a fixed cost now (converting dollars twice) and a yearly cost forever (withholding). The heatmap finds the first year in which the US-listed route is worth at least as much, for dividend yields from 0.5% to 4% and one-way conversion costs from 0.1% to 2%.

With the defaults the answer is 10 years. At a 1.5% yield and a cheap 0.25% conversion it takes 3 years; at a 0.5% yield and a 2% retail spread it takes 57. High-yield holdings and low conversion costs favour the US-listed route; low-yield growth holdings and expensive conversions favour the Canadian-listed fund.

Other differences sit outside this calculation. A US-listed ETF reports in US dollars and needs records of the exchange rate for each purchase and sale in a taxable account; the currency and cost base guide explains why. Large holdings of US-listed securities can also raise US estate tax questions. Simplicity has value too.

06

Chart 4: yield and time decide the size

The last heatmap scales the withholding loss in a registered account to $100,000 for yields from 0.5% to 4% and holding periods from 5 to 40 years. At a 0.5% yield the loss is about $464 after 5 years and $10,520 after 30; at 4% it is about $4,188 after 5 years and over $200,000 after 30, because the lost dividends are a much larger share of the return.

This explains a common rule of thumb: in an RRSP, consider holding the highest-yielding US holdings directly; in a TFSA, which cannot avoid the withholding either way, keep US dividend payers small or hold growth-oriented equities. The asset location guide covers the wider question of what to hold in which account.

Yields change. A US stock index yielding around 1% to 2% is typical of recent decades, but the yield of any fund depends on what it holds and on prices; the figures here are scenarios, not a forecast of income or return.

07

Practical steps

  1. Look at the account first. The account’s tax rules, not the fund, decide whether US withholding can be credited, avoided or not. A fund is not more or less tax-exempt because of the account label on it.
  2. In a taxable account, keep the slips. Claim the foreign tax shown in box 34 of a T3 (or on your broker’s slip) on Form T2209. The credit is limited to the Canadian tax on that foreign income; if your income is very low, part of it may not be usable.
  3. In an RRSP, compare total cost. For a large, long-held US equity position, a US-listed ETF can come out ahead once yield × 15% exceeds the extra yearly fee, and the holding period is long enough to recover the conversion. For small or short holdings the Canadian-listed fund is usually simpler and close in cost.
  4. In a TFSA, FHSA or RESP, do not convert to avoid withholding. It cannot be avoided there. A Canadian-listed fund saves the conversion.
  5. Keep perspective. Diversification, total fees, your risk capacity and staying invested through market falls matter far more over decades than a fraction of a percent. Returns are uncertain and US stocks can fall sharply in Canadian-dollar terms, through both prices and the exchange rate.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. The 15% treaty rate, the pension-trust exemption and the foreign tax credit rules are from the Canada–US tax convention and CRA pages reviewed 26 October 2026. Dividend yield, growth, conversion cost and holding period are hypothetical editable inputs, not the record of any fund. The model leaves out fees, currency movements and tracking differences. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Department of Finance Canada · Convention between Canada and the United States of America with respect to taxes on income and on capital (consolidated to the 2007 Protocol) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026. Article X(2)(b): tax on dividends in the source country not to exceed 15% of the gross amount in all cases other than qualifying intercompany holdings. Article XXI(2): dividends and interest derived by a resident trust, company, organization or other arrangement generally exempt in its home country and operated exclusively to administer or provide pension, retirement or employee benefits are exempt in the other country. The consolidation is unofficial; the Protocols are the legal text.

  2. Canada Revenue Agency · Income Tax Folio S5-F2-C1, Foreign Tax Credit ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026. ¶1.69: foreign taxes paid on foreign income earned on qualifying investments held in an RRSP or through a TFSA arrangement do not count for a foreign tax credit. ¶1.22: for individuals, foreign tax on property income above 15% of that income is deductible under subsection 20(11) rather than creditable.

  3. Canada Revenue Agency · Line 40500 – Federal foreign tax credit ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 (page date 2026-08-14): residents of Canada who include foreign income on their return and paid non-business tax on it to a foreign country can generally claim the credit.

  4. Canada Revenue Agency · Tax treatment of mutual funds ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 (page date 2026-02-05): T3 box 25 foreign non-business income is reported on line 12100 and Form T2209; box 34 foreign non-business income tax paid goes on line 43100 of Form T2209.

  5. Canada Revenue Agency · RC4466, Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA), Guide for Individuals ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026: “If dividend income from a foreign country is paid to a TFSA, the dividend income could be subject to foreign withholding tax.” The page is now marked cancelled; the statement is cited as CRA’s published explanation, not as current guide text.

  6. Canada Revenue Agency · Investments in your FHSAs ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 (page date 2026-02-02): foreign dividends paid to an FHSA could be subject to foreign withholding tax.

  7. Canada Revenue Agency · Current year tax rates and income brackets (2026) ↗

    Reviewed by earlier TickerLantern guides on 25–26 October 2026: federal 20.5% and Ontario 9.15% bracket rates give the 29.65% default combined rate. Your own rate depends on your province and income.
